Wednesday night
Did something small today that felt big. Our office allows two work-from-home days, but I've come in all five days since I joined, just because that's how I started. On Sunday I asked myself: if I were new and there were no pattern yet, what would I pick? Honestly, two home days, to skip the ninety-minute bus ride. My fear was that Yogesh, my manager, would think I'm slacking. So I tested just one day: today. I shared my work by ten o'clock. He replied, "Thanks, looks good." That's it. No raised eyebrow. I finished early and called Mummy, who said her girl sounded less tired. Trying one more next week.
Swati

passage: Every year, the family's soybean crop in their village near Latur went to Seth Ramdas's shop, because that's where Dada had always sold. Sonali, twenty-five and back from her agriculture diploma, asked a simple question at dinner: "If we'd never heard of Ramdas, where would we sell?" Her brother Saurabh laughed. "Where else?" But she had seen the new farmers' collective in town posting higher rates on a board. The fear at the table was real: Ramdas might refuse them next year. So Sonali suggested a test. Just one trolley to the collective, the rest to Ramdas as usual. The collective paid better and on time. Ramdas, when he heard, only said, "Bring the rest."

passage: For two years Katja had taken the 7:40 tram to her job at the Rotterdam library, simply because it was the first route she tried after moving. Her flatmate Omar cycled. "You'd save twenty minutes," he said over toast. "I'd arrive sweaty and soaked," she said, but the question stayed with her. That night she wrote on a sticky note: If I had arrived in this city yesterday, bike or tram? Her honest answer surprised her: bike, at least on dry days. The fear felt real, yet she had never once checked it. On Monday she borrowed Omar's spare bike, left a clean shirt in her locker, and rode in. She arrived four minutes early and only a little warm. By Thursday she had a rule of her own: bike when it's dry, tram when it pours.

qa.q: How did Katja's Monday test answer her fear?

The evening computer class at the Gangtok community centre had always started at six. Nobody remembered why. Dolma, the new programme coordinator, went through the sign-up register one quiet afternoon and saw how many names had "night shift" or "shop closes at 7" written beside them. At the staff meeting she asked, "If we were starting this class today, with these learners, what time would we choose?"
Sahil, who had run the class for three years, crossed his arms. "Change the time and the regulars will drop out."
"Maybe," Dolma said. "Can we check that before we believe it? One extra batch at half past seven, for one month. The six o'clock batch stays."
Sahil agreed, a little stiffly. By the end of the month the six o'clock regulars were all still coming, and the new batch had filled with shopkeepers and hotel workers who had never been able to join.

qa.q: What time had the evening computer class always started?
qa.a: It had always started at six.

qa.q: What was Sahil worried about when Dolma raised the question of timing?
qa.a: He feared that changing the time would make the regulars drop out, which felt like a real risk after running the class for three years.

qa.q: What small step did Dolma choose instead of simply moving the class?
qa.a: She added one extra batch at half past seven for one month while the six o'clock batch stayed, so the feared loss of regulars could be checked.

qa.q: How might the shopkeepers and hotel workers see the new batch?
qa.a: For them it is the first time the class fits their day, so it probably feels like the centre finally noticed people who had never been able to join.

grounding: It shows a decider asking which option she would pick if nothing were the default, and running one small test to see whether the feared cost appears.

passage: I've worked at the district library for eight years, and the hours never changed: ten to six, closed Sundays. When Farida became branch manager, she asked a strange question at her first meeting: "If we were opening this library today, with no old timings, what hours would we pick?" Somebody said evenings, because students and office workers can only come after six. The senior clerk worried nobody would come and that staff would stay late for nothing. Farida didn't argue. She said, "One month, Thursdays only, open till eight. I'll stay myself." I watched her sit at the desk that first Thursday, glancing at the door. By the fourth Thursday, forty-two people came after six. Now even Harsha from the reading room, that's me, volunteers for the late shift.

Monday, 3 June. Nikita stared at the forty-page report the team sent every month. "Why do we do it like this?" she asked Sahil. "Because we always have. The director likes detail." That evening she wrote one line in her notebook: If nobody had ever made this report, what would I build? Her answer was two pages and a link to the full data.
Tuesday, 11 June. She did not scrap the old report. She sent the two-page version to the director with the long one attached and a note: "Trying a shorter format this month. Tell me what's missing." Her stomach knotted as she pressed send.
Friday, 28 June. The director's reply came: "Much easier to read. Add the regional table." The file log showed that the long attachment had not been opened once. Sahil read the reply over her shoulder and whistled softly.

For two years Ankita had taken the same auto route to her Bengaluru office: forty-five minutes, stuck in traffic at Silk Board every morning. When the new metro line opened, everyone said to try it. She kept saying, "My route works."

One Sunday, she caught herself. She took out a notebook and asked: if I had just moved here today, with no habits, which way would I choose?

She wrote both options. Auto: forty-five minutes, unpredictable. Metro: thirty minutes, a ten-minute walk at the end. She'd have chosen the metro without thinking.

So why hadn't she? Because it was new. What if it was crowded? What if she got lost?

She decided to test one small change: metro on Monday and Wednesday, auto the rest of the week.

On Wednesday, she messaged her colleague Binita: "Metro's crowded, but I read twenty pages on the way. I'm switching fully next week."

qa.a: Forty-five minutes.

qa.q: What was Ankita feeling about trying the metro before the test?
qa.a: Ankita felt uneasy and a bit afraid of the new route, worrying it might be crowded or that she might get lost.

qa.q: What two steps did Ankita use to question the default?
qa.a: Ankita asked which route she'd choose with no habits, then tested the metro on two days to see if the feared costs appeared.

I'm Neelam, and I work as a software tester in Chennai. Last year I realised I'd stayed on the same payments-testing team for three years not because I chose it, but because I never chose anything else.

My friend Deepika worked on the accessibility team, making apps usable for blind users. Whenever she talked about it, I felt a pull. But switching felt risky. What if I was bad at it? What if my manager saw it as disloyalty?

One evening, I asked myself a simple question: if I were joining this company today, and both teams were open, which would I pick?

Accessibility. Instantly.

So I didn't quit my team. I asked my manager if I could shadow Deepika's team for two weeks, two afternoons a week. He agreed straight away.

The feared disaster never came. My manager wasn't hurt. I wasn't bad at it. Last month, I moved to the accessibility team for good.

qa.q: How long had Neelam stayed on the payments-testing team?
qa.a: Three years.

qa.q: What was Neelam feeling about switching teams before the shadowing?
qa.a: Neelam felt a pull toward accessibility but also afraid, worrying about being bad at it or looking disloyal.

qa.q: What small test did Neelam run, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Neelam shadowed Deepika's team for two afternoons a week for two weeks, which tested the feared costs without giving up the current role.

qa.q: How might Deepika feel about Neelam joining the team?
qa.a: Deepika probably feels happy and proud, having shared her love of the work.

She brought the sheet to Friday's meeting, and we decided with real evidence instead of habit. My next step: ask her to write up the method for our other two offices.
